name: Priya Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a usual workday involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the viola desk in a regional orchestra, record slow part guides and teach three students. I have a master's degree in music and have spent thirty years settling awkward passages for younger players. I enjoy when the back row hears its line clearly under the melody.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does the work pay at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58, my partner has regular hours at a pharmacy and our children are grown. We rent and have four months of expenses saved. My pay is typical for an orchestra musician and there are some similar posts nearby, but a vacant desk has to be advertised. I use AI occasionally for rehearsal-note drafts after another desk leader tests a tool, then check the score by hand.

I'd say the **viola desk** still needs players listening together.
think: Our **four-month reserve** and partner wage cover one delayed fee.
The **orchestra and lessons** should continue through mild AI.
do: Confirm **six paid calls** and three students; request written cancellation terms.
Check **AI notes** against signed scores and save fifteen percent of an extra cleared fee after essentials.
feel: I feel **calm** while booked calls and household pay remain secure.
S0.quote: A tidy wrong note can spread down an entire desk.
fieldNote: Her **senior viola skill** earns typical pay with four months saved and some nearby orchestras.
Occasional **AI note drafts** are existing use, manually checked against the signed score.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the orchestra a quicker rehearsal note helps if the paid call is still printed beside it. A viola desk needs people listening to each other, not just a neat page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four months saved and my partner's steady pay cover one delayed concert fee. I expect the paid orchestra and teaching work to carry on if AI changes little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll confirm six paid calls and my three students, and ask the manager for written cancellation terms. In the first year of this mild change I'll keep checking occasional AI notes against the signed score and put fifteen percent of an extra cleared concert fee into savings after rent, food and string repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our booked season. A late fee is frustrating, but our bills would still clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened in the snowstorm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A snowstorm moved a concert last winter and the contract paid the rehearsal. We waited for the performance fee, which is why I want dates in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you check a rehearsal note?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I compare every rehearsal note with the marked score and ask the second viola to read the changed bar. A tidy wrong note can spread down an entire desk.

say: I'd ask which **paid hours** for guides and planning software would remove.
I'd bring **fee sheets** to the union before accepting lower preparation pay.
think: Guides and planning bring **one-quarter** of my own pay.
Our **four-month reserve** cannot replace a permanent income cut.
do: Bring **ten guide invoices** to the musicians union this month.
Seek **written live-rehearsal minimum** if fees fall; keep paid calls and students.
Trial **new AI checker** after fee loss/paid off-call demo on owned nameless part with paid-use licence/local approval; play changes, stop errors/leaks.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a realistic cut to preparation pay.
S1.quote: A union meeting can set a rate, but a rate does not create a recording order.
fieldNote: Her **union request** uses invoices to defend paid preparation and rehearsal rates.
A **new AI trial** requires paid instruction, owned nameless music, commercial licence, local storage and manual checks.

steps.text: Bring ten guide invoices to musicians union
Request written paid live-rehearsal minimum if fees fall; keep calls/students
Test checker after fee loss/paid off-call demo on owned nameless part under paid-use licence/local approval

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the manager which paid part-guide and rehearsal-planning hours new software would remove. I'd bring the desk's fee sheets to the musicians union before accepting a lower preparation rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Part guides and planning supply about a quarter of my own pay. If orders shrink, four months saved give me time to respond, but they cannot replace a permanent quarter of income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll compare ten guide invoices with new orders and bring the figures to the union. In the first year, if those fees fall, I'll request a written paid live-rehearsal minimum, keep current calls and students, and attend a paid demonstration of a new AI part checker, which flags wrong written notes, only on my own nameless music with a paid-use licence, approved local storage and manual play-through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a realistic loss of paid preparation. A union meeting can set a rate, but a rate does not create a recording order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check the AI part?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would play every changed bar against paper and stop for wrong notes or a file leaving the orchestra system. A pupil recording stays out without written consent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who pays for the demonstration?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The orchestra must pay the demonstrator without taking my booked rehearsal hour. If the licence does not permit paid use, I will keep the paper part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the viola section that thinking AGI by 2028 could make part guides before a robot plays viola. Playing robots follow around 2031, so I want live calls signed now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect guide and planning fees to end in 2028, taking a quarter of my pay. Live concerts might also be cut, but our current season is booked and I will not count those fees lost yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll total guide and planning income, request signed paid calls and ask for actual pension statements before considering a stop at 60. In the first year after 2028, if live calls also fall, I'll seek a posted paid music-centre ensemble-tutor role only if my master's degree and desk-leading experience qualify, actual in-person ensemble coaching and preparation is paid, and written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and buses fit its hours; I'll keep orchestra and students until a suitable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the expected quarter of my pay disappearing, with four months saved and some local posts giving a search window. I would be alarmed if live concerts fell too, but that is a separate condition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a tutor role open now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No centre has offered me a tutor post. I would read its current paid hours and qualifications before shifting a rehearsal day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you retire at 60?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have not seen our pension statements. A master's degree cannot tell me what pension payment will land in our account each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the orchestra board that five years to AGI by 2031 lets us write paid live desk coaching into the next agreement. Viola-playing robots follow around 2034, but younger players need a leader at rehearsal now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ordinary software could cut guide fees before 2031. My senior title does not automatically pay for the hours I spend marking parts for the section.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next season I'll bring the union a proposed two-year agreement with paid desk-coaching hours, a preparation rate and a cancellation fee. In the first year after 2031, if guide fees stop, I'll keep the booked paid orchestra and student work and ask the union to check each call against the signed agreement; if live dates also fall, I'll seek a posted paid ensemble-tutor role only if my master's and desk-leading history qualify, actual in-person ensemble coaching and preparation is paid, and written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and buses work, keeping current work until a suitable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about guide fees fading, though a written live rate gives us something to enforce. A draft agreement is not pay until the board signs it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has the board agreed to those rates?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the board has not accepted the new rates. The union can present them, but we will budget only signed calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What can the union enforce?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It can compare rehearsal hours and cancelled dates with the signed terms and seek missing fees. It cannot promise an extra concert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my grown children that ten years to AGI by 2036 lets us read real pension figures and paid orchestra terms. Viola-playing robots follow around 2039, but our rent is due before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may still want and need orchestra and student fees. Four months saved now and an unknown pension do not prove we can stop working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll request actual pension statements and a written two-year paid desk-call plan, then save fifteen percent of each extra cleared chamber fee after rent, food and strings toward six months of expenses. In the first year after 2036 I'll keep paid orchestra and student work while booked; if live calls fall and pension figures leave a gap, I'll seek a posted paid ensemble-tutor role only if my master's and desk-leading qualify, actual in-person ensemble coaching and preparation is paid, and written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and buses fit, keeping current work until a suitable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the distant balance of work and retirement while today's calls and four months saved hold. I will decide when to slow paid work using an actual pension amount, not a birthday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no extra chamber fee clears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If no extra chamber job pays, there is no fifteen percent from it to save. I won't move rent money to make six months appear sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you seen your pension amount?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I have not seen our pension statements. I will read them with my partner before dropping a paid rehearsal.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because paid guide and planning work could end before another qualified post opens. Signed orchestra calls, actual pension figures and a posted qualified tutor role with written net pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays the desk leader to mark a difficult passage before rehearsal. An unsigned preparation hour does not put food on the table.

headlineQuote: An unsigned preparation hour does not put food on the table.
portrait: Priya is a **58-year-old viola desk leader** with a music master's degree, partner and grown children.
Her **typical pay**, four-month reserve and some nearby posts offer time to respond if guide fees end.
She uses **AI occasionally** for notes and tests a new checker only after a paid, private and manually checked demonstration.
She seeks **union-backed paid coaching rates** and actual pension figures before reducing booked work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove a quarter of Priya's pay from guides and planning.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed orchestra calls**, actual pension figures and posted qualifying tutoring with written after-travel replacement pay would help.
